newsitem.title: UK: British financial watchdog suspends stockbroker.
newsitem.headline: British financial watchdog suspends stockbroker.

text.p: A stockbroker in the southern English town of Bournemouth who mis-used the accounts of two elderly clients has been suspended and fined by a British financial watchdog.
The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) said on Friday it had acted against David Porter, formerly with Bournemouth-based stockbrokers Robson Cotterell, for "churning" clients' portfolios.

It said Robson Cotterell, which admitted supervisory failings, had been reprimanded, fined 20,000 pounds ($32,100), ordered to pay costs of 10,000 pounds and required to refund a proportion of commission and other charges paid by the two clients.
The SFA said it had suspended Porter from its register for a year. He was also reprimanded, fined 10,000 pounds and ordered to pay 10,360 pounds costs.
Churning is the term used to describe excessive buying and selling of a customer's portfolio, allowing the broker controlling the account to earn extra commission.
Bournemouth, where Porter was employed by Robson Cotterell from 1981 until October 1996, is a south coast seaside resort popular with retired people.

Between January and November 1994, Porter had undertaken 188 and 189 trades on the two accounts. "The overall value of these trades were more than four times the total value of the portfolios," it added.

Porter managed the accounts on a discretionary basis for two elderly sisters. The SFA said during the period in question stocks were repeatedly traded rather than held, with a number of stocks traded on more than four occasions during the period.
It said Porter had also undertaken a number of transactions to establish losses for tax purposes "which were unnecessary as both clients already had substantial brought forward losses".

After a visit by SFA inspectors in September 1994, during which the trading of the accounts was questioned, Porter "devised a letter from a client purporting to thank the firm for its active management of the accounts", the SFA said.
He had then procured the signature of one of the clients to the letter which was returned to the firm in October 1994, it added.

Porter took his case to a disciplinary tribunal which found this was "a deliberately dishonest attempt to justify a course of dealing which he had cause to believe was open to criticism and in respect of which SFA might take action against him".
In deciding the penalty, the tribunal took into account Porter's "hitherto exemplary character", the fact his firm had been disciplined for its failures and that Porter had admitted the charges.
It said that had it not been for these mitigating factors, "the only possible sanction would have been permanent removal from the SFA register".
Porter can only be re-admitted to the register if he successfully passes the appropriate examination and any future employer will have to assure the SFA he would be under close supervision.

In relation to Robson Cotterell, which has been in business for more than 75 years, the SFA said it had taken into account the firm's full cooperation and the fact it had not been disciplined before. ($ = 0.623 British Pounds)
